common_name: Adolphe Audusson Variegated Camellia (Red-and-White Streaked Sport of Adolphe Audusson)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; give it the same generous spacing as its parent 'Adolphe Audusson', since it grows into a large shrub or small tree over time.

directions: Adolphe Audusson Variegated is a naturally occurring branch sport of the classic deep-red 'Adolphe Audusson,' carrying the same large, semi-double flower form and central cluster of golden stamens but with petals irregularly streaked and blotched in white over the blood-red ground, so that no two blooms display quite the same pattern. Because variegated camellia sports are genetically unstable, established plants occasionally throw a branch of solid red flowers reverted to the parent color; prune these out at the base if a consistently marbled display is wanted. It shares its parent's vigorous, upright growth into a large shrub or small tree and blooms on the same mid-season schedule, typically December through February in the Gulf South. Grow it exactly as you would 'Adolphe Audusson' - moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, with a thick mulch layer and protection from hot afternoon sun that can scorch the variegated petal margins.

common_name: Adolphe Audusson Special Camellia (Darker Red Formal Double Sport)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; like its parent, it develops into a large, vigorous shrub or small tree, so allow ample room at planting.

directions: Adolphe Audusson Special is a sport of the widely grown red camellia 'Adolphe Audusson,' distinguished by flowers that open more fully formal and double than the semi-double parent, with tightly imbricated petals in a darker, more saturated red that reads almost black-red in low winter light. It blooms on the same mid-season schedule as its parent and matches its vigorous, upright growth habit, eventually forming a large shrub or small tree in the shaded understory. Because the extra petal count makes flowers heavier and slower to shed spent blooms cleanly, deadheading improves the tidiness of the display without affecting next season's bud set. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with a deep mulch layer, following the same culture as the parent cultivar.

common_name: Elegans Champagne Camellia (White-and-Yellow Anemone-Form Sport of Elegans)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; like its parent 'Elegans,' Elegans Champagne spreads wider than it grows tall, so allow generous width when siting it as a specimen or foundation shrub.

directions: Elegans Champagne is a sport of the historic 1831 cultivar 'Elegans' ('Chandleri Elegans'), keeping the same large anemone-form flower structure - five to six broad outer guard petals surrounding a dense boss of smaller petaloids - but trading the parent's rose-pink coloring for creamy white guard petals set off by soft champagne-yellow petaloids at the center. It shares 'Elegans'' characteristically spreading, wider-than-tall habit and its mid-to-late-season bloom window, making it a good companion planted alongside the pink parent and its other sport, 'Elegans Supreme,' for a succession of related but distinct flower colors from the same historic lineage. Site in morning sun with afternoon shade, moist acidic soil, and a deep mulch layer, and prune only lightly right after flowering since buds set on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Elizabeth Boardman Camellia (Large Pale Pink Semi-Double Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with shelter from wind that can bruise its large petals.

directions: Elizabeth Boardman bears large, semi-double flowers in a soft, pale pink, with broad, slightly ruffled petals surrounding a center of golden stamens, opening over a long midseason window on a vigorous, upright shrub. It is best known today as the seed parent behind the Florida-bred heirloom 'Mrs. D.W. Davis,' whose 1951 seedling went on to win the American Camellia Society's Illges Medal, and it remains grown in its own right among collectors of older Southern camellia cultivars. Give it the same culture as other large-flowered japonicas - moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade with shelter from wind, which can bruise the large, soft petals. Mulch heavily to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist, and prune lightly immediately after bloom to maintain shape without sacrificing next season's flowers.

common_name: William Mohr Iris (Historic 1925 Aril-Medial Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun on a slope or raised bed with sharp drainage; its aril parentage makes it far less tolerant of summer moisture than straight bearded iris.

directions: William Mohr, hybridized by Sydney B. Mitchell and introduced in 1925, was one of the first aril-medial hybrids to reach American gardens, crossing tall bearded iris with an oncocyclus aril species to combine germanica vigor with the huge flower size and dramatic veining typical of arils. Its enormous, rounded, pale lavender-blue flowers are densely veined and stippled in deep reddish-purple, radiating out from a small central signal in a pattern unlike any purebred bearded iris of its era. Though eclipsed in the garden by later introductions, William Mohr's aril blood made it a foundational parent behind decades of aril-medial and large-flowered bearded iris breeding, including the 1945 Dykes Medal winner 'Elmohr.' Because of its aril parentage it appreciates slightly drier, sharper drainage than straight bearded iris and resents summer irrigation, so plant it on a slope or raised bed and withhold water once bloom finishes.

common_name: Dark Boatman Iris (Historic 1949 Dykes Medal Dark Violet-Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Dark Boatman is a historically significant American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris and foundational parent of the modern dark-iris breeding line.

directions: Dark Boatman, hybridized by Paul Cook and introduced in the 1940s, broke new ground as one of the first bearded iris to combine near-black depth of color with a smooth, glowing violet-blue self tone, a combination that made it the standard of comparison for dark iris breeding for a generation. It won the American Dykes Medal in 1949 and went on to become a foundational parent behind many later ultra-dark bearded iris, including the 1964 Dykes Medal winner 'Allegiance,' bred directly from a Dark Boatman cross. The tall, well-branched stems carry the velvety flowers well above the fan of foliage in midseason. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center rhizome and replanting vigorous outer fans in full sun and sharply drained soil.
